entries.c2cac4595c32656f84878902f8c900a906e63a43: <div sID="gen4541" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="23" osisID="Josh.23" sID="Josh.23"/> <div eID="gen4541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4542" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4543" type="x-p"/> In this and the following chapter we have two farewell sermons, which Joshua preached to the people of Israel a little before his death. Had he designed to gratify the curiosity of succeeding ages, he would rather have recorded the method of Israel's settlement in their new conquests, their husbandry, manufacturers, trade, customs, courts of justice, and the constitutions of their infant commonwealth, which one would wish to be informed of; but that which he intended in the registers of this book was to entail on posterity a sense of religion and their duty to God; and therefore, overlooking these things which are the usual subjects of a common history, he here transmits to his reader the methods he took to persuade Israel to be faithful to their covenant with their God, which might have a good influence on the generations to come who should read those reasonings, as we may hope they had on that generation which then heard them. In this chapter we have, I. A convention of the states called (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.1-Josh.23.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>), probably to consult about the common concerns of their land, and to set in order that which, after some years' trial, being left to their prudence, was found wanting. II. Joshua's speech to them as the opening, or perhaps at the concluding, of the sessions, to hear which was the principal design of their coming together. In it, 1. Joshua reminds them of what God had done for them (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.3-Josh.23.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.9">9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.14">14</reference>), and what he was ready to do yet further, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.5">ver. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.10">10</reference>. 2. He exhorts them carefully and resolutely to persevere in their duty to God, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.6">ver. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.8">8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.11">11</reference>. III. He cautions them against all familiarity with their idolatrous neighbours, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.7">ver. 7</reference>. IV. He gives them fair warning of the fatal consequences of it, if they should revolt from God and turn to idols, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.12-Josh.23.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.15">15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.16">16</reference>. In all this he showed himself zealous for his God, and jealous over Israel with a godly jealousy.
entries.e994677dce0d59740721e82ced2c140c5fddd1d8: <div eID="gen4543" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4542" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Joshua's Charge to Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1427.)</title> <div sID="gen4544" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass a long time after that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had given rest unto Israel from all their enemies round about, that Joshua waxed old <hi type="italic">and</hi> stricken in age. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Joshua called for all Israel, <hi type="italic">and</hi> for their elders, and for their heads, and for their judges, and for their officers, and said unto them, I am old <hi type="italic">and</hi> stricken in age: <hi type="super">3</hi> And ye have seen all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God hath done unto all these nations because of you; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that hath fought for you. <hi type="super">4</hi> Behold, I have divided unto you by lot these nations that remain, to be an inheritance for your tribes, from Jordan, with all the nations that I have cut off, even unto the great sea westward. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, he shall expel them from before you, and drive them from out of your sight; and ye shall possess their land, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God hath promised unto you. <hi type="super">6</hi> Be ye therefore very courageous to keep and to do all that is written in the book of the law of Moses, that ye turn not aside therefrom <hi type="italic">to</hi> the right hand or <hi type="italic">to</hi> the left; <hi type="super">7</hi> That ye come not among these nations, these that remain among you; neither make mention of the name of their gods, nor cause to swear <hi type="italic">by them,</hi> neither serve them, nor bow yourselves unto them: <hi type="super">8</hi> But cleave unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, as ye have done unto this day. <hi type="super">9</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath driven out from before you great nations and strong: but <hi type="italic">as for</hi> you, no man hath been able to stand before you unto this day. <hi type="super">10</hi> One man of you shall chase a thousand: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, he <hi type="italic">it is</hi> that fighteth for you, as he hath promised you. <div eID="gen4544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4545" type="x-p"/> As to the date of this edict of Joshua, <div eID="gen4545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4546" type="x-p"/> I. No mention at all is made of the place where this general assembly was held; some think it was at Timnath-serah, Joshua's own city, where he lived, and whence, being old, he could not well remove. But it does not appear that he took so much state upon him; therefore it is more probable this meeting was at Shiloh, where the tabernacle of meeting was, and to which place, perhaps, all the males that could had now come up to worship before the Lord, at one of the three great feasts, which Joshua took the opportunity of, for the delivering of this charge to them. <div eID="gen4546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4547" type="x-p"/> II. There is only a general mention of the time when this was done. It was <hi type="italic">long after the Lord had given them rest,</hi> but it is not said how long, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.1">v. 1</reference>. It was, 1. So long as that Israel had time to feel the comforts of their rest and possessions in Canaan, and to enjoy the advantages of that good land. 2. So long as that Joshua had time to observe which ways their danger lay of being corrupted, namely, by their intimacy with the Canaanites that remained, against which he is therefore careful to arm them. <div eID="gen4547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4548" type="x-p"/> III. The persons to whom Joshua made this speech: <hi type="italic">To all Israel, even their elders, &c.</hi> So it might be read, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.2">v. 2</reference>. They could not all come within hearing, but he called for all the elders, that is, the privy-counsellors, which in later times constituted the great Sanhedrim, the heads of the tribes, that is, the noblemen and gentlemen of their respective countries, the judges learned in the laws, that tried criminals and causes, and gave judgment upon them, and, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> the officers or sheriffs, who were entrusted with the execution of those judgments. These Joshua called together, and to them he addressed himself, 1. That they might communicate what he said, or at least the sense and substance of it, to those under them in their respective countries, and so this charge might be dispersed through the whole nation. 2. Because, if they would be prevailed upon to serve God and cleave to him, they, by their influence on the common people, would keep them faithful. If great men be good men, they will help to make many good. <div eID="gen4548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4549" type="x-p"/> IV. Joshua's circumstances when he gave them this charge: He <hi type="italic">was old and stricken in age</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.1">v. 1</reference>), probably it was in the last year of his life, and he lived to be 110 years old, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.29">ch. xxiv. 29</reference>. And he himself takes notice of it, in the first words of his discourse, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.2">v. 2</reference>. When he began to be old, some years ago, God reminded him of it (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.1">ch. xiii. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art old.</hi> But now he did himself feel so much of the decays of age that he needed not to be told of it, he readily speaks of it himself: <hi type="italic">I am old and stricken in age.</hi> He uses it, 1. As an argument with himself to give them this charge, because being old he could expect to be but a little while with them, to advise and instruct them, and therefore (as Peter speaks, <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.13">2 Pet. i. 13</reference>) <hi type="italic">as long as he is in this tabernacle</hi> he will take all opportunities to <hi type="italic">put them in remembrance</hi> of their duty, knowing by the increasing infirmities of age that he must shortly put off this tabernacle, and desiring that after his decease they might continue as good as they were now. When we see death hastening towards us, this should quicken us to do the work of life with all our might. 2. As an argument with them to give heed to what he said. He was old and experienced, and therefore to be the more regarded, for days should speak; he had grown old in their service, and had spent himself for their good, and therefore was to be the more regarded by them. He was old and dying; they would not have him long to preach to them; therefore let them observe what he said now, and lay it up in store for the time to come. <div eID="gen4549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4550" type="x-p"/> V. The discourse itself, the scope of which is to engage them if possible, them and their seed after them, to persevere in the true faith and worship of the God of Israel. <div eID="gen4550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4551" type="x-p"/> 1. He puts them in mind of the great things God had done for them, now in his days, and under his administration, for here he goes no further back. And for the proof of this he appeals to their own eyes (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You have seen all that the Lord your God has done;</hi> not what I have done, or what you have done (we were only instruments in God's hand), but what God himself has done by me and for you." (1.) Many great and mighty nations (as the rate of nations then went) were driven out from as fine a country as any was at that time upon the face of the earth, to make room for Israel. "You see <hi type="italic">what he has done to these nations,</hi> who were his creatures, the work of his hands, and whom he could have made new creatures and fit for his service; yet see what destruction he has made of them <hi type="italic">because of you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.2">v. 2</reference>), how he has <hi type="italic">driven them out from before you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.9">v. 9</reference>), as if they were of no account with him, though great and strong in comparison with you." (2.) They were not only driven out (this they might have been, and yet sent to some other country less rich to begin a new plantation there, suppose to that wilderness in which Israel had wandered so long, and so they would only have exchanged seats with them), but they were trodden down before them; though they held out against them with the greatest obstinacy that could be, yet they were subdued before them, which made the possessing of their land so much the more glorious to Israel and so much the more illustrious an instance of the power and goodness of the God of Israel (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord your God</hi> has not only led you, and fed you, and kept you, but he has fought for you as a man of war," by which title he was known among them when he first brought them out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.3">Exod. xv. 3</reference>. So clear and cheap were all their victories, during the course of this long war, that <hi type="italic">no man had been able to stand before them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.9">v. 9</reference>), that is, to make head against them, so as to put them in fear, create them any difficulty, or give any check to the progress of their victorious arms. In every battle they carried the day, and in every siege they carried the city; their loss before Ai was upon a particular occasion, was inconsiderable, and only served to show them on what terms they stood with God; but, otherwise, never was army crowned with such a constant uninterrupted series of successes as the armies of Israel were in the wars of Canaan. (3.) They had not only conquered the Canaanites, but were put in full possession of their land (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have divided to you by lot these nations,</hi> both those which are cut off and those which remain, not only that you may spoil and plunder them, and live at discretion in their country for a time, but to be a sure and lasting inheritance for your tribes. You have it not only under your feet, but in your hands." <div eID="gen4551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4552" type="x-p"/> 2. He assures them of God's readiness to carry on and complete this glorious work in due time. It is true some of the Canaanites did yet remain, and in some places were strong and daring, but this should be no disappointment to their expectations; when Israel was so multiplied as to be able to replenish this land God would expel the Canaanites to the last man, provided Israel would pursue their advantages and carry on the war against them with vigour (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord your God will drive them from out of your sight,</hi> so that there shall not be a Canaanite to be seen in the land; and even that part of the country which is yet in their hands you shall possess." If it were objected that the men of war of the several tribes being dispersed to their respective countries, and the army disbanded, it would be difficult to get them together when there was occasion to renew the war upon the remainder of the Canaanites, in answer to this he tells them what little need they had to be in care about the numbers of their forces (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">One man of you shall chase a thousand,</hi> as Jonathan did, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.13">1 Sam. xiv. 13</reference>. "Each tribe may venture for itself, and for the recovery of its own lot, without fearing disadvantage by the disproportion of numbers; for the Lord your God, whose all power is, both to inspirit and to dispirit, and who has all the creatures at his beck, <hi type="italic">he it is that fighteth for you;</hi> and how many do you reckon him for?" <div eID="gen4552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4553" type="x-p"/> 3. He hereupon most earnestly charges them to adhere to their duty, to go on and persevere in the good ways of the Lord wherein they had so well set out. He exhorts them, <div eID="gen4553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4554" type="x-p"/> (1.) To be very courageous (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.6">v. 6</reference>): "God fighteth for you against your enemies, do you therefore <hi type="italic">behave yourselves valiantly</hi> for him. Keep and do with a firm resolution <hi type="italic">all that is written in the book of the law.</hi>" He presses upon them no more than what they were already bound to. "Keep with care, do with diligence, and eye what is written with sincerity." <div eID="gen4554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4555" type="x-p"/> (2.) To be very cautious: "Take heed of missing it, either on the right hand or on the left, for there are errors and extremes on both hands. Take heed of running either into a profane neglect of any of God's institutions or into a superstitious addition of any of your own inventions." They must especially take heed of all approaches towards idolatry, the sin to which they were first inclined and would be most tempted, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.7">v. 7</reference>. [1.] They must not acquaint themselves with idolaters, nor come among them to visit them or be present at any of their feasts or entertainments, for they could not contract any intimacy nor keep up any conversation with them, without danger of infection. [2.] They must not show the least respect to any idol, nor <hi type="italic">make mention of the name of their gods,</hi> but endeavour to bury the remembrance of them in perpetual oblivion, that the worship of them may never be revived. "Let the very name of them be forgotten. Look upon idols as filthy detestable things, not to be named without the utmost loathing and detestation." The Jews would not suffer their children to name swine's flesh, because it was forbidden, lest the name of it should occasion their desiring it; but, if they had occasion to speak of it, they must call it <hi type="italic">that strange thing.</hi> It is a pity that among Christians the names of the heathen gods are so commonly used, and made so familiar as they are, especially in plays and poems: let those names which have been set up in rivalship with God be for ever loathed and lost. [3.] They must not countenance others in showing respect to them. They must not only not swear by them themselves, but they must not cause others to swear by them, which supposes that they must not make any covenants with idolaters, because they, in the confirming of their covenants, would swear by their idols; never let Israelites admit such an oath. [4.] They must take heed of these occasions of idolatry, lest by degrees they should arrive at the highest step of it, which was serving false gods, and bowing down to them, against the letter of the second commandment. <div eID="gen4555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4556" type="x-p"/> (3.) To be very constant (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Cleave unto the Lord your God,</hi> that is, "delight in him, depend upon him, devote yourselves to his glory, and continue to do so to the end, <hi type="italic">as you have done unto this day,</hi> ever since you came to Canaan;" for, being willing to make the best of them, he looks not so far back as the iniquity of Peor. There might be many things amiss among them, but they had not forsaken the Lord their God, and it is in order to insinuate his exhortation to perseverance with the more pleasing power that he praises them. "Go on and prosper, for the Lord is with you while you are with him." Those that command should commend; the way to make people better is to make the best of them. "You have cleaved to the Lord unto this day, therefore go on to do so, else you lose the praise and recompence of what you have wrought. Your righteousness will not be mentioned unto you if you turn from it."
entries.2c2c3179340f9942fbd2245ba3307cda6392ba30: <div eID="gen4556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4557" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Take good heed therefore unto yourselves, that ye love the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <hi type="super">12</hi> Else if ye do in any wise go back, and cleave unto the remnant of these nations, <hi type="italic">even</hi> these that remain among you, and shall make marriages with them, and go in unto them, and they to you: <hi type="super">13</hi> Know for a certainty that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God will no more drive out <hi type="italic">any of</hi> these nations from before you; but they shall be snares and traps unto you, and scourges in your sides, and thorns in your eyes, until ye perish from off this good land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God hath given you. <hi type="super">14</hi> And, behold, this day I <hi type="italic">am</hi> going the way of all the earth: and ye know in all your hearts and in all your souls, that not one thing hath failed of all the good things which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God spake concerning you; all are come to pass unto you, <hi type="italic">and</hi> not one thing hath failed thereof. <hi type="super">15</hi> Therefore it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> as all good things are come upon you, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God promised you; so shall the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> bring upon you all evil things, until he have destroyed you from off this good land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God hath given you. <hi type="super">16</hi> When ye have transgressed the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, which he commanded you, and have gone and served other gods, and bowed yourselves to them; then shall the anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> be kindled against you, and ye shall perish quickly from off the good land which he hath given unto you. <div eID="gen4557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4558" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Joshua directs them what to do, that they might persevere in religion, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.11">v. 11</reference>. Would we cleave to the Lord, and not forsake him, 1. We must always stand upon our guard, for many a precious soul is lost and ruined through carelessness: "Take heed therefore, <hi type="italic">take good heed to yourselves,</hi> to your <hi type="italic">souls</hi> (so the word is), that the inward man be kept clean from the pollutions of sin, and closely employed in the service of God." God has given us precious souls with this charge, "Take good heed to them, keep them with all diligence, above all keepings." 2. What we do in religion we must do from a principle of love, not by constraint or from a slavish fear of God, but of choice and with delight. "<hi type="italic">Lord the Lord your God,</hi> and you will not leave him." <div eID="gen4558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4559" type="x-p"/> II. He urges God's fidelity to them as an argument why they should be faithful to him (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I am going the way of all the earth,</hi> I am old and dying." To die is to go a journey, a journey to our long home; it is the way of all the earth, the way that all mankind must go, sooner or later. Joshua himself, though so great and good a man, and one that could so ill be spared, cannot be exempted from this common lot. He takes notice of it here that they might look upon these as his dying words, and regard them accordingly. Or thus: "<hi type="italic">I am dying,</hi> and leaving you. <hi type="italic">Me you have not always;</hi> but if you cleave to the Lord he will never leave you." Or thus, "Now that I am near my end it is proper to look back upon the years that are past; and, in the review, I find, and you <hi type="italic">yourselves know it in all your hearts and in all your souls,</hi> by a full conviction on the clearest evidence, and the thing has made an impression upon you"—(that knowledge does us good which is seated, not in the head only, but in the heart and soul, and with which we are duly affected)—"you know that <hi type="italic">not one thing hath failed of all the good things which the Lord spoke concerning you</hi>" (and he spoke a great many); see <reference osisRef="Josh.21.45">ch. xxi. 45</reference>. God had promised them victory, rest, plenty, his tabernacle among them, &c., and <hi type="italic">not one thing had failed</hi> of all he had promised. "Now," said he, "has God been thus true to you? Be not you false to him." It is the apostle's argument for perseverance (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.23">Heb. x. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">He is faithful that has promised.</hi> <div eID="gen4559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4560" type="x-p"/> III. He gives them fair warning what would be the fatal consequences of apostasy (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.12-Josh.23.13">v. 12, 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.15">15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.16">16</reference>): "If you go back, know for a certainty it will be your ruin." Observe, <div eID="gen4560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4561" type="x-p"/> 1. How he describes the apostasy which he warns them against. The steps of it would be (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.12">v. 12</reference>) growing intimate with idolaters, who would craftily wheedle them, and insinuate themselves into their acquaintance, now that they had become lords of the country, to serve their own ends. The next step would be intermarrying with them, drawn to it by their artifices, who would be glad to bestow their children upon these wealthy Israelites. And the consequence of that would be (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.16">v. 16</reference>) <hi type="italic">serving other gods</hi> (which were pretended to be the ancient deities of the country) and bowing down to them. Thus the way of sin is down-hill, and those who have fellowship with sinners cannot avoid having fellowship with sin. This he represents, (1.) As a base and shameful desertion; "it is going back from what you have so well begun," <reference osisRef="Josh.23.12">v. 12</reference>. (2.) As a most perfidious breach of promise (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.16">v. 16</reference>): "It is a transgression of <hi type="italic">the covenant of the Lord your God, which he commanded you,</hi> and which you yourselves set your hand to." Other sins were transgressions of the law God commanded them, but this was a transgression of the covenant he commanded them, and amounted to a breach of the relation between God and them and a forfeiture of all the benefits of the covenant. <div eID="gen4561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4562" type="x-p"/> 2. How he describes the destruction which he warns them of. He tells them, (1.) That these remainders of the Canaanites, if they should harbour them, and indulge them, and join in affinity with them, would be snares and traps to them, both to draw them to sin (not only to idolatry, but to all immoralities, which would be the ruin, not only of their virtue, but of their wisdom and sense, their spirit and honour), and also to draw them into foolish bargains, unprofitable projects, and all manner of inconveniences; and having thus by underhand practices decoyed them into one mischief or other, so as to gain advantages against them, they would then act more openly, and be <hi type="italic">scourges in their sides</hi> and <hi type="italic">thorns in their eyes,</hi> would perhaps kill or drive away their cattle, burn or steal their corn, alarm or plunder their houses, and would be all ways possible be vexatious to them; for, whatever pretences of friendship they might make, a Canaanite, unless proselyted to the faith and worship of the true God, would in every age hate the very name and sight of an Israelite. See how the punishment would be made to answer the sin, nay, how the sin itself would be the punishment. (2.) That the anger of the Lord would be kindled against them. Their making leagues with the Canaanites would not only give those idolaters the opportunity of doing them a mischief, and be the fostering of snakes in their bosoms, but it would likewise provoke God to become their enemy, and would kindle the fire of his displeasure against them. (3.) That all the threatenings of the word would be fulfilled, as the promise had been, for the God of eternal truth is faithful to both (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.15">v. 15</reference>): "<hi type="italic">As all good things have come upon you</hi> according to the promise, so long as you have kept close to God, so all evil things will come upon you according to the threatening, if you forsake him." Moses had <hi type="italic">set before them good and evil;</hi> they had experienced the good, and were now in the enjoyment of it, and the evil would as certainly come if they were disobedient. As God's promises are not a fool's paradise, so his threatenings are not bugbears. (4.) That it would end in the utter ruin of their church and nation, as Moses had foretold. This is three times mentioned here. Your enemies will vex you <hi type="italic">until you perish from off this good land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.23.13">v. 13</reference>. Again, "God will plague you <hi type="italic">until he have destroyed you from off this good land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.23.15">v. 15</reference>. Heaven and earth will concur to root you out, so that (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.16">v. 16</reference>) <hi type="italic">you shall perish from off the good land.</hi>" It will aggravate their perdition that the land from which they shall perish is a good land, and a land which God himself had given them, and which therefore he would have secured to them if they by their wickedness had not thrown themselves out of it. Thus the goodness of the heavenly Canaan, and the free and sure grant God has made of it, will aggravate the misery of those that shall for ever be shut out and perish from it. Nothing will make them see how wretched they are so much as to see how happy they might have been. Joshua thus sets before them the fatal consequences of their apostasy, that, <hi type="italic">knowing the terror of the Lord,</hi> they might be persuaded <hi type="italic">with purpose of heart to cleave to him.</hi>  <chapter eID="Josh.23"/> <div eID="gen4562" type="x-p"/>

entries.37065ba3ff4b4e6d7adc71aca93ab6063318e7b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2180"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 23</title> <div sID="gen2927" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Josh.23.1">Jos 23:1</reference>, 2. Joshua's Exhortation before His Death.<div eID="gen2927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2928" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2180"/><hi type="bold">1. a long time after that the Lord had given rest unto Israel from all their enemies--</hi>about fourteen years after the conquest of Canaan, and seven after the distribution of that country among the tribes. <div eID="gen2928" type="x-p"/>
entries.41cc6fd946e2433cc31e737adbf5da0effab8169: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2181"/><div sID="gen2929" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2181"/><hi type="bold">2. Joshua called for all Israel--</hi>The clause which follows seems to restrict this general expression as applicable only to the officers and representatives of the people. The place of assembly was most probably Shiloh. The occasion of convening it was the extreme age and approaching death of the venerable leader; and the purport of this solemn address was to animate the chosen people and their posterity to a faithful and unswerving continuance in the faith and worship of the God of Israel. <div eID="gen2929" type="x-p"/>
entries.d00c567811d85e13712f3e65fb1370c768c9a03e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2182"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.23.3">Jos 23:3</reference>. By Former Benefits.</title> <div sID="gen2930" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2182"/><hi type="bold">3. ye have seen all that the Lord your God hath done unto all these nations because of you--</hi>The modesty and humility of Joshua are remarkably displayed at the commencement of this address. Dismissing all thoughts of his personal services, he ascribed the subjugation and occupation of Canaan entirely to the favoring presence and aid of God; and in doing so, he spoke not more piously than truly. This had been promised (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.30">De 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.22">3:22</reference>); and the reality of the divine aid was seen in the rapid overthrow of the Canaanites, which had already led to the division of the whole land among the tribes [Jos 23:4]. <div eID="gen2930" type="x-p"/>
entries.79cca0acd3bf626bbb61847891792a74f6aaf55c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2183"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.23.5-Josh.23.11">Jos 23:5-11</reference>. By Promises.</title> <div sID="gen2931" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2183"/><hi type="bold">5-11. the Lord your God, he shall expel them from before you, as the Lord your God hath promised you, &c.--</hi>The actual possessions which God had given were a pledge of the complete fulfilment of His promise in giving them the parts of the country still unconquered. But the accomplishment of the divine promise depended on their inviolable fidelity to God's law--on their keeping resolutely aloof from all familiar intercourse and intimate connections with the Canaanites, or in any way partaking of their idolatrous sins. In the event of their continuing in steadfast adherence to the cause of God, as happily distinguished the nation at that time, His blessing would secure them a course of brilliant and easy victories (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.7">Le 26:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.7">De 28:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.30">32:30</reference>). <div eID="gen2931" type="x-p"/>
entries.daa822cafb04650244e569cd3a3ed1cffa757455: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2185"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.23.12">Jos 23:12</reference>. By Threatenings in Case of Disobedience.</title> <div sID="gen2933" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2185"/><hi type="bold">12-13. Else if ye do in any wise go back, and cleave unto the remnant of these nations--</hi>As marriage connections with the idolatrous Canaanites would present many and strong temptations to transgress it, these were strictly prohibited (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.12-Exod.34.16">Ex 34:12-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.3">De 7:3</reference>). With his eye, as it were, upon those prohibitions, Joshua threatens them with the certain withdrawal of the divine aid in the further expulsion of the Canaanites (a threat founded <reference osisRef="Exod.23.33">Ex 23:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.33.55">Nu 33:55</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.16">De 7:16</reference>). <chapter eID="Josh.23"/>

entries.ca3ca142f787cde8091466446928646e1358e55a: <div eID="gen8218" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen8219" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8220" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8220" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8219" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8221" type="x-p"/> Joshua, being old, calls for the rulers and different heads of the Israelites, <reference osisRef="Jos.23.1">Jos 23:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.23.2">Jos 23:2</reference>, to whom he relates how God had put them in possession of the promised land, <reference osisRef="Jos.23.3">Jos 23:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.23.4">Jos 23:4</reference>; from which all their remaining enemies should be expelled, <reference osisRef="Jos.23.5">Jos 23:5</reference>. Exhorts them to be faithful to God, and to avoid all connections with the idolatrous nations, <reference osisRef="Jos.23.6-Jos.23.8">Jos 23:6-8</reference>. Encourages them with the strongest promises, that no enemy should ever be able to prevail against them, if they continued to love the Lord their God, <reference osisRef="Jos.23.9-Jos.23.11">Jos 23:9-11</reference>. Lays also before them the consequences of disobedience, <reference osisRef="Jos.23.12">Jos 23:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.23.13">Jos 23:13</reference>. Shows them that as all God's promises had been fulfilled to them while they were obedient, so his threatening should be fulfilled own them if they revolted from his service; and that if they did so, they should be utterly destroyed from off the good land, <reference osisRef="Jos.23.14-Jos.23.16">Jos 23:14-16</reference>. <div eID="gen8221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8222" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen8222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8223" type="x-p"/> A long time after that the Lord had given rest - This is supposed to have been in the last or one hundred and tenth year of the life of Joshua, about thirteen or fourteen years after the conquest of Canaan, and seven after the division of the land among the tribes.
entries.dc84e494891edad9ea77ec600d003336e5011c69: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen8223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8224" type="x-p"/> Joshua called for all Israel - There are four degrees of civil distinction mentioned here: <div eID="gen8224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8225" type="x-p"/> 1. זקנים zekenim, the elders or senate, the Princes of the tribes. <div eID="gen8225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8226" type="x-p"/> 2. ראשים rashim or rashey aboth, the Chiefs or Heads of families. <div eID="gen8226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8227" type="x-p"/> 3. שפטים shophetim, the Judges who interpreted and decided according to the law. <div eID="gen8227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8228" type="x-p"/> 4. שטרים shoterim, the Officers, serjeants, etc., who executed the decisions of the judges. <div eID="gen8228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8229" type="x-p"/> Whether this assembly was held at Timnath-serah, where Joshua lived, or at Shiloh, where the ark was, or at Shechem, as in <reference osisRef="Jos.24.1">Jos 24:1</reference>, we cannot tell. Some think that the meaning here, and that mentioned in <reference osisRef="Jos.24.1">Jos 24:1</reference>, were the same, and if so, Shechem was the place of assembling; but it is more likely that the two chapters treat of two distinct assemblies, whether held at the same place or not.
entries.e5a029550ba9ed1fa58de78ad1817c6391b16752: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen8229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8230" type="x-p"/> For the Lord your God is he that hath fought for you - There is much both of piety and modesty in this address. It was natural for the Israelites to look on their veteran, worn-out general, who had led them on from conquest to conquest, with profound respect; and to be ready to say, "Had we not had such a commander, we had never got possession of this good land." Joshua corrects this opinion, and shows them that all their enemies had been defeated, because the Lord their God had fought for them. That the battle was the Lord's, and not his; and that God alone should have the glory.
entries.7e00a6bf69bbe94194da5adb65d7d171470c4c73: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen8230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8231" type="x-p"/> I have divided - these nations that remain - The whole of the promised land had been portioned out, as well those parts which had not yet been conquered, as those from which the ancient inhabitants had been expelled. The Canaanitish armies had long ago been broken in pieces, so that they could make no head against the Israelites, but in many districts the old inhabitants remained, more through the supineness of the Israelites, than through their own bravery. <div eID="gen8231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8232" type="x-p"/> From Jordan - unto the great sea - All the land that lay between the river Jordan, from Phiala, where it rose, to the southern extremity of the Dead Sea, and to the Mediterranean Sea, through the whole extent of its coast, opposite to Jordan.
entries.e3ee6b612abcd7bd52f1772e9b18c530f5b8f2e4: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen8232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8233" type="x-p"/> And drive them - out - and ye shall possess - The same Hebrew word ירש yarash is used here to signify to expel from an inheritance, and to succeed those thus expelled. Ye shall disinherit them from your sight, and ye shall inherit their land.
entries.410e10fad5103ef511091918b4b2fdd9f137e8b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen8233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8234" type="x-p"/> Be ye therefore very courageous to keep and to do, etc. - It requires no small courage to keep a sound creed in the midst of scoffers, and not less to maintain a godly practice among the profane and profligate. <div eID="gen8234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8235" type="x-p"/> That is written in the book - By the word of God alone his followers are bound. Nothing is to be received as an article of faith which God has not spoken.
entries.b43bab61e4783df1a33c783df7521ef1f1b28181: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen8235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8236" type="x-p"/> Come not among these nations - Have no civil or social contracts with them, (see <reference osisRef="Jos.23.12">Jos 23:12</reference>), as these will infallibly lead to spiritual affinities, in consequence of which ye will make honorable mention of the name of their gods, swear by them as the judges of your motives and actions, serve them in their abominable rites, and bow yourselves unto them as your creators and preservers; thus giving the whole worship of God to idols: and all this will follow from simply coming among them. He who walks in the counsel of the ungodly will soon stand in the way of sinners, and shortly sit in the seat of the scornful. Nemo repente fuit turpissimus. "No man rises to the highest stages of iniquity but by degrees." Nero himself, under the instructions of Seneca, was a promising youth.
entries.8594c5ffab84db7fcd02da89eb124125f83b68e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen8236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8237" type="x-p"/> One man of you shall chase a thousand - Do not remain inactive on the supposition that you must be much more numerous before you can drive out your enemies, for it is the Lord that shall drive out nations great and strong; and under his direction and influence one of you shall chase a thousand.
entries.46cc960103e2db3b2cec74db377fdfa4fd5420aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen8237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8238" type="x-p"/> Take good heed - unto yourselves that ye love the Lord - לנפשתיכם lenaphshotheychem, Take heed To Your Souls, literally; but נפש nephesh and nefs, both in Hebrew and Arabic, signify the whole self, as well as soul and life; both soul and body must be joined in this work, for it is written, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, soul, mind, and strength.
entries.ca51c6daa432576ad2c912ecc955169bb46329c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen8238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8239" type="x-p"/> Else if ye do - go back - The soldier who draws back when going to meet the enemy, forfeits his life. These were the Lord's soldiers, and if they drew back they drew back unto perdition, their lives being forfeited by their infidelity.
entries.4a4302fb47faf4abace1c220bca37469655f90b8: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen8239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8240" type="x-p"/> They shall be snares - לפח lephach, a net or gin, set by the artful fowler to catch heedless birds. <div eID="gen8240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8241" type="x-p"/> And traps - מוקש mokesh, any snare, toil, or trap, placed on the ground to catch the unwary traveler or wild beast by the foot. <div eID="gen8241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8242" type="x-p"/> Scourges in your sides, and thorns in your eyes - Nothing can be conceived more vexatious and distressing than a continual goad in the side, or thorn in the eye. They will drive you into obedience to their false gods, and put out the eyes of your understandings by their idolatries. And God will preserve them merely to distress and punish you.
entries.50a2fefbd8495e037dca8dbdff754b5253458298: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen8242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8243" type="x-p"/> The way of all the earth - I am about to die; I am going into the grave. <div eID="gen8243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8244" type="x-p"/> Not one thing hath failed, etc. - God had so remarkably and literally fulfilled his promises, that not one of his enemies could state that even the smallest of them had not had its most literal accomplishment: this all Israel could testify.
entries.2d477997c039f73c143b7d6412d3b713705401ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen8244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8245" type="x-p"/> So shall the Lord bring upon you all evil things - His faithfulness in fulfilling his promises is a proof that he will as faithfully accomplish his threatenings, for the veracity of God is equally pledged for both.
entries.7000e8614896469764f41943d1e8d5c868caedd1: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen8245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8246" type="x-p"/> Ye shall perish quickly from off the good land - The following note from Mr. John Trapp is very judicious: "This judgment Joshua inculcates <reference osisRef="Jos.23.13">Jos 23:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.23.15">Jos 23:15</reference>, and here, because he knew it would be a very grievous thing to them to forego so goodly a land, so lately gotten, and so short a while enjoyed. In the beginning of a speech τα ηθη, the milder affections, suit best; but towards the end τα παθη, passionate and piercing passages; according to the orator. This rule Joshua observes, being Ex utroque Caesar; no less an orator than a warrior." <div eID="gen8246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8247" type="x-p"/> In all this exhortation we see how closely Joshua copies the example of his great master Moses. See <reference osisRef="Lev.26.7">Lev 26:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.8">Lev 26:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.14">Lev 26:14</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Deu.28.7">Deu 28:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.32.30">Deu 32:30</reference>. He was tenderly concerned for the welfare of the people, and with a deeply affected heart he spoke to their hearts. No people ever were more fairly and fully warned, and no people profited less by it. The threatenings pronounced here were accomplished in the Babylonish captivity, but more fully in their general dispersion since the crucifixion of our Lord. And should not every Christian fear when he reads, If God spared not the natural branches, take heed that he spare not thee? Surely a worldly, carnal, and godless Christian has no more reason to expect indulgence from the justice of God than a profligate Jew. We have a goodly land, but the justice of God can decree a captivity from it, or a state of bondage in it. The privileges that are abused are thereby forfeited. And this is as applicable to the individual as to the whole system.  <chapter eID="Josh.23"/> <div eID="gen8247" type="x-p"/>

entries.3b9d4dc86f021a64a126e44ed71b4ea679b3acdc: <div eID="gen3002" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Joshua’s Farewell and Death - Joshua 23-24</title> <div sID="gen3003" type="x-p"/> After the division of the land among the tribes, Joshua had withdrawn to <hi type="italic">Timnath-serah</hi>, on the mountains of Ephraim (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.50">Jos 19:50</reference>), to spend the last days of his life there in the quiet enjoyment of his own inheritance. But when the time of his departure from the earth was drawing near, remembering the call which he had received from the Lord (<reference osisRef="Josh.1.6-Josh.1.8">Jos 1:6-8</reference>), he felt constrained to gather the people together once more in the persons of their representatives, to warn them most earnestly of the dangers of apostasy from the Lord, and point out the evils that would follow (Josh 23); and then after that, in a solemn assembly of the nation at Shechem, to review the abundant mercies which the Lord had conferred upon Israel from the calling of Abraham to that day, that he might call upon them to remain stedfast and faithful in the worship of their God, and then solemnly renew the covenant with the Lord.<note placement="foot">“The pious solicitude of Joshua furnishes an example worthy of imitation by all who have the charge of others. For just as a father would not be regarded as sufficiently careful it he merely thought of the interests of his children up to the time of his own death, and did not extend his thoughtfulness on their behalf still further, and as far as was in his power endeavour to provide for their welfare when he himself should be dead; so good rulers ought to look forward that they may not only leave behind them a well-organized state, but may also strengthen and secure its existence for a long time to come.” - <hi type="italic">Calvin</hi> (with special reference to 2Pe 1:13-15).</note> <div eID="gen3003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3004" type="x-p"/> Exhortation to the Tribes of Israel to Remain Faithful to their Calling. - <reference osisRef="Josh.23.1">Jos 23:1</reference>, Jos 23:2. The introduction to the discourse which follows is attached in its first part to <reference osisRef="Josh.22.3-Josh.22.4">Jos 22:3-4</reference>, and thus also to <reference osisRef="Josh.21.43-Josh.21.44">Jos 21:43-44</reference>, whilst in the second part it points back to Jos 13:1. The Lord had given the people rest from all their enemies round about, after the land had been subdued and divided by lot (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.43-Josh.21.44">Jos 21:43-44</reference>). Joshua was already an old man at the termination of the war (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.1">Jos 13:1</reference>); but since then he had advanced still further in age, so that he may have noticed the signs of the near approach of death. He therefore called together the representatives of the people, either to Timnath-serah where he dwelt (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.50">Jos 19:50</reference>), or to Shiloh to the tabernacle, the central sanctuary of the whole nation, as the most suitable place for his purpose. “<hi type="italic">All Israel</hi>” is still further defined by the apposition, “<hi type="italic">its elders, and its heads, and its judges, and its officers</hi>.” This is not to be understood, however, as referring to four different classes of rulers; but the term <hi type="italic">elders</hi> is the general term used to denote all the representatives of the people, who were divided into heads, judges, and officers. And the <hi type="italic">heads</hi>, again, were those who stood at the head of the tribes, families, and fathers’ houses, and out of whose number the most suitable persons were chosen as judges and officers (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.15">Deu 1:15</reference>; see my Bibl. Arch. ii. § 143). Joshua’s address to the elders of all Israel consists of two parts, which run parallel to one another so far as the contents are concerned, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.2-Josh.23.13">Jos 23:2-13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.23.14">Jos 23:14</reference>-16. In both parts Joshua commences with a reference to his age and his approaching death, in consequence of which he felt constrained to remind the people once more of all the great things that the Lord had done for them, and to warn them against falling away from their gracious covenant God. Just as Joshua, in this the last act of his life, was merely treading in the footsteps of Moses, who had concluded his life with the fullest exhortations to the people to be faithful to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.30">Deu 1:30</reference>), so his address consists entirely of reminiscences from the Pentateuch, more especially from Deuteronomy as he had nothing fresh to announce to the people, but could only impress the old truth upon their minds once more. <div eID="gen3004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3005" type="x-p"/> Joshua commenced his address by reminding them of the greatest manifestations of grace which they had received from the Lord, namely, by referring to what the Lord had done to all these nations (the Canaanites) before them, when He fought for Israel, as Moses had promised them (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.30">Deu 1:30</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.3.22">Deu 3:22</reference>).
entries.04078d041119804011d682a6b945c65468f89c7f: <reference osisRef="Josh.23.3">Jos 23:3</reference> <div eID="gen3005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3006" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Before you</hi>,” sc., smiting and driving them away.
entries.8f39ab0b65d816abdce98ad20b17708092c03020: <reference osisRef="Josh.23.4">Jos 23:4</reference> <div eID="gen3006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3007" type="x-p"/> He (Joshua) had now divided by lot among the tribes of Israel as their inheritance these still remaining (Canaanitish) nations, as the Lord had commanded (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.6-Josh.13.7">Jos 13:6-7</reference>), “<hi type="italic">from Jordan and further all the nations, which I have exterminated</hi> (i.e., which Joshua had destroyed when Canaan was taken), <hi type="italic">and the great sea</hi> (for 'to the great sea') <hi type="italic">in the west</hi>.” The breadth of the land of Canaan is here given in a peculiar manner, the <hi type="italic">terminus a quo</hi> being mentioned in the first clause, and the <hi type="italic">terminus ad quem</hi> (though without the preposition עד) in the second; and through the parallelism which exists between the clauses, each clause is left to be completed from the other. So that the whole sentence would read thus: “<hi type="italic">All these nations which remain ... from Jordan to the great sea, also all the nations which I have cut off from Jordan, and to the great sea westward</hi>.”
entries.5e6431e885475100dde19a8d862679ed1d705c22: <reference osisRef="Josh.23.5">Jos 23:5</reference> <div eID="gen3007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3008" type="x-p"/> For the Lord would drive all these still remaining nations before the Israelites, and cut them off, and give the Israelites their land for a possession, as He had promised (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.6">Jos 13:6</reference>; cf. Exo 23:23.). הדף, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.6.19">Deu 6:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.4">Deu 9:4</reference>; and the form יהדּפם, with <hi type="italic">Chateph-kametz</hi>, on account of the weakness of the ה, as in Num 35:20. ירשׁתּם, as in Jos 1:15.
entries.1e6916ac57332ea9f12c1f7d6346cc2c92f8d619: <reference osisRef="Josh.23.6-Josh.23.8">Jos 23:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen3008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3009" type="x-p"/> Only let them be strong, i.e., be brave, to keep the law of Moses without fail (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.1.7">Jos 1:7</reference>), to enter into no fellowship with these remaining nations (בּוא, to enter into close intimacy with a person; see <reference osisRef="Josh.23.12">Jos 23:12</reference>), and not to pay reverence to their gods in any way, but to adhere stedfastly to the Lord their God as they had hitherto done. To make mention of the names of the idols (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.13">Exo 23:13</reference>), to swear by them, to serve them (by sacrifices), and to bow down to them (to invoke them in prayer), are the four outward forms of divine worship (see <reference osisRef="Deut.6.13">Deu 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.10.20">Deu 10:20</reference>). The concluding words, “<hi type="italic">as ye have done unto this day</hi>,” which express a reason for persevering in the attachment they had hitherto shown to Jehovah, “do not affirm that the Israelites had hitherto done all these things fully and perfectly; for who does not know how few mortals there are who devote themselves to God with all the piety and love which He justly demands? But because the nation as a whole had kept the laws delivered to them by Moses, during the time that the government had been in the hands of Joshua, the sins of individual men were left out of sight on this occasion” (<hi type="italic">Masius</hi>).
entries.5f46ae477cc7858db84f88c5269229fef56e483d: <reference osisRef="Josh.23.9-Josh.23.13">Jos 23:9-13</reference> <div eID="gen3009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3010" type="x-p"/> For this reason the Lord had driven out great and strong nations before the Israelites, so that no one was able to stand before them. The first hemistich points to the fulfilment of <reference osisRef="Deut.4.38">Deu 4:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.1">Deu 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.1">Deu 9:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.23">Deu 11:23</reference>; the second to that of <reference osisRef="Deut.7.24">Deu 7:24</reference>; Deu 11:25. ואתּם is placed at the beginning absolutely. - In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Josh.23.10">Jos 23:10</reference></hi>, the blessing of fidelity to the law which Israel had hitherto experienced, is described, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.30">Deu 32:30</reference>, upon the basis of the promise in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.7-Lev.26.8">Lev 26:7-8</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.28.7">Deu 28:7</reference>, and in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Josh.23.10">Jos 23:10</reference></hi> the thought of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Josh.23.3">Jos 23:3</reference></hi> is repeated. To this there is attached, in <reference osisRef="Josh.23.11-Josh.23.13">Jos 23:11-13</reference>, the admonition to take heed for the sake of their souls (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.4.15">Deu 4:15</reference>), to love the Lord their God (on the love of God as the sum of the fulfilment of the law, see <reference osisRef="Deut.6.5">Deu 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.10.12">Deu 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.13">Deu 11:13</reference>). For if they turned, i.e., gave up the faithfulness they had hitherto displayed towards Jehovah, and attached themselves to the remnant of these nations, made marriages with them, and entered into fellowship with them, which the Lord had expressly forbidden (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.12-Exod.34.15">Exo 34:12-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.3">Deu 7:3</reference>), let them know that the Lord their God would not cut off these nations before them any more, but that they would be a snare and destruction to them. This threat is founded upon such passages of the law as <reference osisRef="Exod.23.33">Exo 23:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.16">Deu 7:16</reference>, and more especially Num 33:55. The figure of a trap, which is employed here (see <reference osisRef="Exod.10.7">Exo 10:7</reference>), is still further strengthened by פּח, a <hi type="italic">snare</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.8.14-Isa.8.15">Isa 8:14-15</reference>). <hi type="italic">Shotet</hi>, a <hi type="italic">whip</hi> or <hi type="italic">scourge</hi>, an emphatic form of the word derived from the <hi type="italic">poel</hi> of שׁוּט, only occurs here. “<hi type="italic">Scourges in your sides, and thorns in your eyes</hi>” (see Num 33:55). Joshua crowds his figures together to depict the misery and oppression which would be sure to result from fellowship with the Canaanites, because, from his knowledge of the fickleness of the people, and the wickedness of the human heart in its natural state, he could foresee that the apostasy of the nation from the Lord, which Moses had foretold, would take place but too quickly; as it actually did, according to Jdg 2:3., in the very next generation. The words “<hi type="italic">until ye perish</hi>,” etc., resume the threat held out by Moses in <reference osisRef="Deut.11.17">Deu 11:17</reference> (cf. Josh Deu 28:21.). <div eID="gen3010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3011" type="x-p"/> In the second part of his address, Joshua sums up briefly and concisely the leading thoughts of the first part, giving greater prominence, however, to the curse which would follow apostasy from the Lord.
entries.0dfe401fbd8a5eb7dbf4205512dd1e331902ec18: <reference osisRef="Josh.23.14-Josh.23.16">Jos 23:14-16</reference> <div eID="gen3011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3012" type="x-p"/> Now that Joshua was going the way of all the earth (all the inhabitants of the earth), i.e., going to die (1Ki 2:2), the Israelites knew with all the heart and all the soul, i.e., were fully convinced, that of all the good words (gracious promises) of God not one had failed, but all had come to pass (vid., <reference osisRef="Josh.21.45">Jos 21:45</reference>). But it was just as certain that the Lord would bring upon them every evil word that He spake through Moses (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.14-Lev.26.33">Lev 26:14-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.15-Deut.28.68">Deut 28:15-68</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.29.14-Deut.29.28">Deu 29:14-28</reference>), if they transgressed His covenant. “<hi type="italic">The evil word</hi>” is the curse of rejection (<reference osisRef="Deut.30.1">Deu 30:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.30.15">Deu 30:15</reference>). “<hi type="italic">Until He have destroyed:</hi>” see <reference osisRef="Deut.7.24">Deu 7:24</reference>, and Deu 28:48. The other words as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Josh.23.13">Jos 23:13</reference></hi>. If they went after other gods and served them, the wrath of the Lord would burn against them, and they would be quickly destroyed from the good land which He had given them (vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.11.17">Deu 11:17</reference>).  <chapter eID="Josh.23"/> <div eID="gen3012" type="x-p"/>

entries.32564a19db47ad937f262dea028356042e5089e1: <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.23.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Josh.23.1" sID="gen24618" type="section"/> <div sID="gen24619" type="x-p"/>Here we have a narrative of the solemn protestation which Joshua used towards the time of his death, that he might leave the pure worship of God surviving him. But although the peace and quiet which the Israelites obtained among the nations of Canaan is described as an excellent blessing from God, it is necessary to keep in mind what I formerly taught, that it was owing to their cowardice that they dwelt among their enemies, whom it would not have been difficult to rout and destroy. But thanks are justly rendered to God for his goodness in pardoning their ingratitude.<div eID="gen24619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24620" type="x-p"/>The pious solicitude of Joshua is here also set forth, for the imitation of all who are in authority. For as the father of a family will not be considered sufficiently provident if he thinks of his children only till the end of his own life, and does not extend his care farther, studying as much as in him lies to do them good even when he is dead; so good magistrates and rulers ought carefully to provide that the well arranged condition of affairs as they leave them, be confirmed and prolonged to a distant period. For this reason Peter writes, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Pet.1.15">2 Peter 1:15</reference>) <note n="189"> <div sID="gen24621" type="x-p"/> The original text had the reference to <reference osisRef="Bible:2Pet.1.25">2 Peter 1:25</reference>, an obvious typesetting error. —<hi type="italic">fj.</hi><div eID="gen24621" type="x-p"/> </note> that he will endeavor after he has departed out of the world to keep the Church in remembrance of his admonitions, and able to derive benefit from them.<div eID="gen24620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24622" type="x-p"/>From its being said that he invited all Israel, and its being immediately after added that he invited their elders, and heads, and judges, and prefects, I understand the meaning to be that all were indeed permitted to come, but that the summons was addressed specially to the heads and prefects. And thus the last clause appears to me to be explanatory of the former. And, indeed, it is not at all credible that the whole people were invited; for no such meeting could possibly take place. The sense, therefore, in which the people were invited was simply this, that the elders, judges, and others were commanded to come, and might bring as many persons as were disposed to come along with them.<div eID="gen24622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24623" type="x-p"/>The speech of Joshua, as quoted, is double; but it appears to me that the historian first, as is often done, gives a brief summary of the whole speech, and then follows it out more in detail, introducing the particulars which he had omitted. <note n="190"> <div sID="gen24624" type="x-p"/> According to this view, the details given in <reference osisRef="Bible:Josh.23">Joshua 23</reference> and <reference osisRef="Bible:Josh.24">Joshua 24</reference> refer only to one meeting. It may be so, but certainly the impression produced by a simple perusal of the chapters is, that they refer to two distinct meetings, between which some interval of time must have elapsed. It is only by means of labored criticism, accompanied with a degree of straining, that some expositors have arrived at a different conclusion. But why should it be deemed necessary to employ criticism for such a purpose? There is surely no antecedent improbability that Joshua, after all the turmoil’s of war were over, should have more than once come forth from his retirement, and called the heads of the people, or even the whole body of them together to receive his counsels, when he felt that the time of his departure was at hand. Observe, moreover, that each meeting is ushered in by its own appropriate preamble, and has its own special business. In the one, Joshua speaks in his own name, and delivers his own message; in the other, all the tribes are regularly assembled, and are said to have “presented themselves before God,” because, although Joshua was still to be the speaker, he was no longer to speak in his own name, but with the authority of a divine messenger, and in the very terms which had been put into his mouth. Accordingly, the very first words he utters are, “Thus said the Lord God of Israel.” The message thus formally and solemnly announced in <reference osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.2">Joshua 24:2</reference>, is continued verbatim and without interruption to the end of <reference osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.13">Joshua 24:13</reference>. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen24624" type="x-p"/> </note> In the one which is first given, Joshua briefly animates the people, and exhorts them to sure confidence in the continued and unwearying grace of God. For, seeing they had experienced that God is true in all things, they could have no doubt for the future, that they might safely hope for the same success in vanquishing and destroying the enemy. The partition also by which he had distributed the remainder of the land, he set before them as an earnest or pledge of their undoubted fruition, because it was not at random but by the order of God he had marked out the seat, and fixed the boundaries of each tribe.<div eID="gen24623" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.23.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen24618" osisID="Josh.23.1" type="section"/>
entries.f9b86e66b94f0182cc2135a8a420ca03611801f4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.23.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Josh.23.6" sID="gen24625" type="section"/> <div sID="gen24626" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6.</hi> <hi type="italic">Be you therefore very courageous, </hi>etc He now shows them the mode of conquering, — not to indulge gross security, as too often happens, as a substitute for genuine confidence. He affirms that God will be propitious to them, and promises that whatever they attempt will turn out prosperously, provided they are steadfast in obeying the Law. However confidently hypocrites may contemn and deride God, they would wish, however, to have him astricted to them; nay, they often, with no small pomposity, boast of his promises. But true faith, while it reclines upon God, keeps those who possess it in his fear. In short, those who would find God must seek him sincerely, and if we desire to be regarded by him, we must beware of turning our backs upon him. The expression, Be you very courageous, as has elsewhere been said, denotes serious study, because in the great weakness of our nature no man will set about the thorough observance of the Law, if he does not exert himself above his strength. Attention ought also to be paid to the definition of true obedience which is here repeated from Moses, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.5.32">Deuteronomy 5:32</reference>) and said to consist in not turning either to the right hand or the left.<div eID="gen24626" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.23.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen24625" osisID="Josh.23.6" type="section"/>
entries.3500545b887b5c9efcaca245ff1bff386c8b31f9: <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.23.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Josh.23.7" sID="gen24627" type="section"/> <div sID="gen24628" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7.</hi> <hi type="italic">That you come not among these nations, </hi>etc He distinctly admonishes them that it will be impossible rightly to discharge their duty if they be not carefully on their guard against all sources of corruption. This it was very necessary to enforce upon them. For they were surrounded on all sides by the snares of Satan, and we know how great their proneness to superstition was, or rather how headlong their eagerness for it. First, then, he warns them that intimate intercourse with the nations may involve them in fellowship in crime; for the term <hi type="italic">mingling </hi>used in this passage is equivalent to what is termed by St. Paul, <hi type="italic">being yoked. </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.6.14">2 Corinthians 6:14</reference>) In short, he first removes the incitements or allurements to idolatry, and then declares his detestation of idolatry itself. It is to be observed, however, that he does not expressly mention either bending of the knee, or sacrifices, or other rites, but designates all perverse modes of worship by the terms <hi type="italic">naming </hi>them and <hi type="italic">swearing </hi>by them. Whence we infer that God is defrauded of his honor when ever any particle, however small, of all the things which he claims for himself is transferred to idols. He accordingly concludes that they are to adhere to God alone; in other words, they are to be bound to him out and out.<div eID="gen24628" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.23.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen24627" osisID="Josh.23.7" type="section"/>

9. For the Lord has driven out from before you, etc He intimates that so long as they do not themselves change, there will certainly be no change on the part of God. Therefore he asserts that, provided they conciliate the favor of God, they shall have an uninterrupted course of victory. At length he again exhorts them, as they value their life and safety, to be careful in maintaining love to God. From this source all true obedience springs; for if we do not cling to him with free and ardent affection, we shall study in vain to frame our lives in accordance with the external form of the Law.
Joshua 23:12-16
12. Else if you do in any wise go back, and cleave unto the remnant of these nations, even these that remain among you, and shall make marriages with them, and go in unto them, and they to you:
12. Quia si avertendo aversi fueritis, et adhaeseritis residuis gentibus istis, residuis, inquam, istis quae sunt vobiscum: et affinitatem contraxeritis cum eis, et misceatis vos cum eis, et ipsae vobiscum:

14. And, behold, this day I am going the way of all the earth: and you know in all your hearts and in all your souls, that not one thing has failed of all the good things which the LORD your God spoke concerning you; all are come to pass unto you, and not one thing has failed thereof.
14. En autem ego ingredior hodie viam universae terrae: cognoscite ergo toto corde vestro, et tota anima vestra quod non cecidit verbum unum ex omnibus verbis optimis quae loquutus est Jehova Deus vester super vos: omnia evenerunt vobis, non cecidit ex eis verbum unum.
